design_detail: Before–after comparison of calendar periods in four markers of heroin use and harm in western Canada, with no comparison place or series. The authors take the Australian heroin shortage to have begun in about January 2001 (citing an earlier review) and state as their primary hypothesis that Canadian markers would stay stable or rise after it. Three routine series are compared as yearly averages, with no statistical test: drug-induced deaths in the whole province of British Columbia from the provincial vital statistics agency (1998–2000 against 2001–03); ambulance responses that required naloxone in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside (fiscal years 1997–98 to 2000–01 against 2001–02 to 2002–03); and the weight of heroin destined for Canada that was seized, from a Royal Canadian Mounted Police report (1998–2000 against 2001–03). In VIDUS, a prospective cohort of people who inject drugs in Vancouver interviewed every 6 months, self-reported daily heroin injection at 13,609 observations (6-monthly interviews) of 1,587 participants (May 1996 to December 2004) is compared between 2001–04 and 1996–2000 by repeated-measures logistic regression (generalized estimating equations, GEE), adjusted for individual characteristics. Filed as prospective-cohort, the design of its only analysis with statistics; the other three series are aggregate counts. No figures for 2005, none for Vancouver's overdose deaths or for any area smaller than the Downtown Eastside, and no mention of supervised injection.
can_establish: Whether four markers of heroin use and harm in western Canada (drug-induced deaths in British Columbia, naloxone-requiring ambulance responses in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside, heroin seized for Canada, and self-reported daily heroin injection in a Vancouver cohort of people who inject drugs) were lower in 2001–03 (2001–04 for the cohort) than in the late 1990s, by how much, and, from the yearly figures, when each began to fall.
cannot_establish: That heroin supply, availability or purity fell, or why (none was measured; seizures may mark enforcement as well as supply, and the deaths include other drugs); that the falls began with the Australian shortage (deaths and naloxone use were already falling from 1998 and fiscal 1998–99); or anything about 2005, about Vancouver's overdose deaths, or about the area around the supervised injection site that opened in Vancouver in September 2003, which the paper does not mention.

sample.recruitment: Routine statistics: drug-induced deaths in British Columbia registered by the provincial vital statistics agency, 1998–2003 (ref. 19); ambulance responses that required naloxone in the Downtown Eastside, fiscal years 1997–98 to 2002–03 (the data's source is not named; the text cites two of the team's earlier papers for regular counting of naloxone use in the area, refs 2 and 20); heroin destined for Canada that was seized, 1998–2003 (a Royal Canadian Mounted Police report, ref. 22) (p. 690). Cohort: VIDUS, an ongoing prospective cohort of people who inject drugs in Vancouver since May 1996, described in earlier papers (refs 23–24); interviewer-administered questionnaire and blood sample at baseline and every 6 months; 1,587 participants gave 13,609 observations at which daily heroin use could be assessed, May 1996 to December 2004 (pp. 690–691).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not given for the cohort in this paper (earlier descriptions cited). Routine series as defined by each agency; the deaths are all drug-induced deaths, the drug not specified (p. 690).
sample.demographics: Not reported. Age, gender, Aboriginal ethnicity and Downtown Eastside residence enter the cohort model, but their distribution is not given (Table 2, p. 693).
sample.attrition: Not reported: interviews per period, loss to follow-up, deaths and enrolment after 2000 are not given.
sample.selection_effects: The cohort is a community cohort of people who inject drugs, recruited as described elsewhere and followed as it aged; who stayed in it and who joined later may differ between periods, which the paper does not report. The four markers describe different populations: the whole province (deaths), the Downtown Eastside (naloxone, chosen because most of the province's overdoses occur there and its naloxone data are counted regularly), all of Canada (seizures) and the cohort.

exposure.measurement: The exposure is calendar time: the period from January 2001, the authors' date for the start of the Australian heroin shortage (citing Degenhardt et al., 2005), stands for a fall in heroin supply that is not itself measured. Seizures are offered as a potential indicator of supply and, the authors note, could also mark supply-reduction (enforcement) activity (p. 690). The authors write that Canada has no standardized longitudinal measures of street heroin purity (p. 694); no price or availability data are used.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable (comparison of periods). The cohort outcome, daily heroin injection, is self-reported at 6-monthly interviews.
exposure.polysubstance: The deaths are all drug-induced deaths, not attributed to a drug; the authors expect some not to involve heroin (p. 690). The cohort model adjusts for daily cocaine injection and daily crack use; the authors say other drugs did not fall similarly and methamphetamine use rose significantly over the period, with no data shown (p. 691).

comparison.controls: Earlier years of the same series (1998–2000; fiscal 1997–98 to 2000–01; 1996–2000 in the cohort). No comparison place and no series unaffected by the supposed supply change; Australia appears only through other authors' reports.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Trends already under way before 2001 are not modelled: in Figure 1, deaths fall from 1998 and naloxone use from fiscal 1998–99 (p. 692). The routine series are counts without population denominators, and changes in treatment, policing, ambulance practice and the cohort's age and make-up are not measured. Canadian supply-reduction funding and activity are said to be unchanged since the mid-1990s on the strength of one citation (ref. 16), with no data shown.

outcomes.instruments: Provincial vital statistics counts of drug-induced deaths; ambulance counts of responses requiring naloxone; Royal Canadian Mounted Police figures for heroin seized; interviewer-administered questionnaire on daily drug use in VIDUS.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors say overdose statistics and seizure data may be poor proxies for heroin use and that the four measures were not counted at the same level; they cite other studies in which ambulance and overdose mortality statistics correlated strongly with street heroin purity (pp. 693–694). Self-reported daily heroin injection is not validated in this paper.
outcomes.operationalization: A fall in heroin supply is inferred from falls in the four markers. Heroin-related harm is drug-induced deaths (any drug) and naloxone-requiring ambulance responses; heroin use is self-reported daily heroin injection. The routine series are yearly counts, although the text calls them rates (pp. 690–691).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; only the cohort comparison has a statistical test.

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 1 (p. 691), yearly averages: drug-induced deaths 297 (1998–2000) against 192 (2001–03), a 35.4% reduction; naloxone-requiring responses 674 (fiscal 1997–98 to 2000–01) against 370 (2001–02 to 2002–03), 45.1%; heroin seized 184 kg against 67 kg, 63.6%; no intervals or tests (the percentages reproduce from the averages, editors' calculation). Cohort (Table 2, p. 693): daily heroin injection in 2001–04 against 1996–2000, adjusted odds ratio 0.55 (95% CI 0.50 to 0.61), P<0.001; shares reporting daily use 36.5% (1997/98), 32.6% (1999/00), 23.3% (2001/02) and 20.8% (2003/04), without counts or denominators (p. 691). Editors' reading of Figure 1 (p. 692) at 300 dpi, approximate (bar tops read inside the 0.96-point bar outlines against the axis ticks; the bar rectangles drawn in the PDF agree within 1): deaths about 399, 272, 218, 221, 169 and 186 (1998 to 2003); naloxone-requiring responses about 732, 840, 655, 464, 388 and 350 (fiscal 1997–98 to 2002–03); heroin seized about 234, 142, 177, 94, 46 and 60 kg (1998 to 2003). Means of these readings by period: 296 and 192 deaths, 673 and 369 responses, 184 and 67 kg, each within 1 of Table 1. Editors' calculations from the readings: deaths fell about 45% from 1998 to 2000 (about four-fifths of the fall from 1998 to the lowest year, 2002), were about the same in 2001 as in 2000, and the 2001–03 mean was about 12% below 2000; naloxone-requiring responses fell about 45% from fiscal 1998–99 to 2000–01 and about 20% from 2000–01 to the mean of the next two years; seizures fell about 47% from 2000 to 2001. Steps in the cohort's daily use: −3.9, −9.3 and −2.5 percentage points between successive two-year periods.
analysis.covariates: Cohort model: period, daily cocaine injection (adjusted odds ratio 2.32, 2.08 to 2.60), daily crack use (1.85, 1.65 to 2.06), sex-trade involvement (1.34, 1.20 to 1.52), current methadone use (0.43, 0.37 to 0.51), and age, Downtown Eastside residence, Aboriginal ethnicity and gender (no estimates shown; all P<0.05 in the final model); variables entered if P ≤ 0.05 in univariate GEE; behaviours time-updated (p. 691; Table 2, p. 693). Routine series: none.
analysis.preregistration_detail: An a priori statistical protocol is mentioned (p. 691); it is not published or registered.
analysis.selective_reporting: Trends for methamphetamine and other drugs are summarized with 'data not shown' (p. 691); the cohort is reported only as one odds ratio and four two-year shares, and the visual inspection said to confirm its trend is not shown; period boundaries follow the date of the Australian shortage and differ between series (calendar years, fiscal years, 1996–2000 against 2001–04).
analysis.power: Not reported. The cohort estimate is precise (interval 0.50 to 0.61); the routine series have no statistical comparison.

interpretation_gap.results_show: All four markers were lower after 2000 than in the late 1990s. The yearly figures show deaths and naloxone use falling from 1998 and fiscal 1998–99, with most of the fall in deaths before 2001 (about 399 in 1998, 218 in 2000, 221 in 2001, and 169 and 186 in 2002 and 2003; editors' reading); seizures were lower in each year from 2001 (about 94, 46 and 60 kg) than in any earlier year (about 234, 142 and 177 kg), and the cohort's largest step in daily heroin injection came between 1999/00 and 2001/02. Nothing measures heroin purity, price or availability, the deaths include other drugs, and the data end in 2003 (2004 for the cohort).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and summary describe massive decreases in independent markers of heroin use coinciding with the Australian shortage despite no increase in Canadian enforcement funding, and conclude that external global heroin supply forces deserve greater investigation and credence (pp. 689, 694); the discussion finds the Canadian shortage “so clearly evident in these crude data” (p. 693). Gaps: (1) the paper does not mention that its own Figure 1 shows deaths and naloxone use falling about two years before 2001, so the period comparison partly measures an earlier trend; (2) deaths and naloxone responses are markers of overdose, not of use, and are not independent of each other; (3) the fall in seizures, which the authors say could also mark enforcement activity, is read as a fall in supply, while unchanged Canadian enforcement rests on one citation (ref. 16) with no data; (4) the statement that reduced heroin availability on Vancouver's streets was widely reported in the media cites a study of HIV viral rebound (ref. 17); (5) no measure of purity, price or availability is used, which the authors acknowledge (p. 694).

timeline.event: Same cohort (VIDUS) and four of the same authors: the share reporting a non-fatal overdose in the previous 6 months fell from 21% in 1997 to 6% in 2004, the largest decline placed during 2001; the authors cite this paper and suggest reduced heroin supply may have played a role (not an independent replication)

Evaluation of the Vancouver supervised injection site, with three of this paper's authors, cites it (ref. 44, p. 1434) for drug use largely constant from 2001 to 2005, daily heroin injecting 24% in 2001 and 25% in 2005, daily cocaine injecting 17% and 15%, and stable methadone use; none of these figures is in this paper, whose data end in 2004
A published letter on that evaluation cites this paper, dated 2004 there, for higher heroin availability until 2001 that declined by 2002 and stayed low (its ref. 3)
The evaluators' reply cites a different 2006 paper by the same five authors (Addiction 101, 623–625) and a 2009 web report for daily heroin use stable from 2001 to 2005; neither is on file

replication.where_it_stands: The only source on file for yearly drug-induced deaths in British Columbia, naloxone-requiring ambulance responses in the Downtown Eastside and Canadian heroin seizures around 2001. Its finding that these markers were lower after 2000 fits the same cohort's fall in reported non-fatal overdoses (Kerr et al., 2007; same team, not independent). Whether heroin supply fell, and why, is not measured in these papers. Both sides of the dispute over the Vancouver supervised injection site cite it: the critics for higher availability until 2001, the evaluators for stable drug use from 2001 to 2005, figures it does not contain.

funding.funder: VIDUS is supported by the US National Institutes of Health (R01 DA011591–04A1) and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (MOP-67262) (Acknowledgements, p. 694); no other funding statement.
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: All five authors at the British Columbia Centre for Excellence in HIV/AIDS, St Paul's Hospital, Vancouver; three also at the Department of Medicine, University of British Columbia (p. 689). Three of them (Wood, Montaner, Kerr) are also authors of the 2011 evaluation of the Vancouver supervised injection site that cites this paper. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Yearly measures of heroin purity, price and availability in Vancouver (for example, laboratory analysis of street samples) from the late 1990s to 2005, with overdose deaths by drug and by area, analysed as an interrupted time series that models the trend before 2001 and compares a market with no change in supply.

domains.note: Two-period averages with no adjustment and no comparison series; trends already under way in the paper's own figure (deaths from 1998, naloxone use from fiscal 1998–99) are not modelled; changes in population, treatment, policing and ambulance practice are not measured for the routine series. The cohort model adjusts for individual characteristics but has no term for time in the cohort, ageing or turnover, so its period term carries every other change between the late 1990s and 2001–04.

The exposure that matters, a fall in heroin supply, is not measured: it is assumed from the date given for the Australian shortage. Seizures, the only supply marker, may also mark enforcement. The naloxone fiscal years place some months of 2001 in the before period (4 months, by the authors' account).
The routine series are complete counts at their level; the cohort is a community cohort whose make-up across periods (who stayed, who joined) is not reported.

Methadone use is adjusted for in the cohort only; other changes during 2001–04, such as the Downtown Eastside police crackdown of April 2003 and the supervised injection site of September 2003 (both described in other papers on file), are not considered.
For the cohort, interviews per period, loss to follow-up and missing answers are not reported.
Deaths are drug-induced deaths from any drug; naloxone use depends on ambulance practice; daily heroin injection is self-reported. Counts without population denominators.
Period boundaries are set by the date of the Australian shortage and differ between series; other drug trends are not shown; the cohort is reported only as one odds ratio and four two-year shares.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E is used because the paper relates calendar periods, standing for a change in heroin supply, to markers of heroin use and harm (METHODS §5.3). High overall, from confounding by trends already under way, visible in the paper's own figure, and from an exposure that is assumed, not measured; for any inference that heroin supply fell from 2001, a stricter reading would give very high. Within that, the counts come from routine sources and the cohort analysis is large and adjusted for individual characteristics. Citable for: the yearly averages of Table 1; the yearly values of Figure 1 as the editors' approximate readings, including that deaths fell mostly before 2001 and that 2001 was about level with 2000 and above 2002 and 2003; and the cohort's self-reported daily heroin injection (adjusted odds ratio 0.55 for 2001–04 against 1996–2000; 36.5%, 32.6%, 23.3% and 20.8% for 1997/98 to 2003/04). Not citable for: a measured fall in heroin supply, availability, purity or price; a fall beginning in 2001; any figure for 2005, for Vancouver's overdose deaths or for the area around the supervised injection site.

key_findings.finding: The authors take the Australian heroin shortage to have begun in about January 2001 and hypothesize that, because western Canada receives heroin from similar source countries and (citing one paper, ref. 16) had not changed its supply-reduction funding or strategies, Canadian markers of heroin-related harm would stay stable or rise after it.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Aims (p. 689); Introduction, 3rd paragraph, and Methods › Assumptions and hypothesis, 1st paragraph (p. 690)

key_findings.finding: Data sources: drug-induced deaths for the whole of British Columbia, 1998–2003, from the provincial vital statistics agency (the drugs responsible were not available, and the authors expect some deaths not to involve heroin); ambulance responses requiring naloxone in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside, by fiscal year, 1997–98 to 2002–03; heroin destined for Canada that was seized, 1998–2003, as a potential indicator of supply that could also mark supply-reduction activity. Periods compared: 1998–2000 against 2001–03; for naloxone, four fiscal years (1997–98 to 2000–01) against two (2001–02 to 2002–03).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data sources, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (right column)

key_findings.finding: Cohort analysis: VIDUS questionnaire data from May 1996 to December 2004; daily heroin use at each 6-monthly interview related to the period (1996–2000 against 2001–04) by GEE logistic regression, with age, gender, ethnicity, daily cocaine injection, daily crack use, sex-trade involvement, methadone use and Downtown Eastside residence considered as confounders, under an a priori protocol entering variables with P ≤ 0.05 in univariate analyses.

Yearly averages (Table 1): drug-induced deaths in British Columbia 297 in 1998–2000 against 192 in 2001–03 (35.4% reduction); naloxone-requiring ambulance responses in the Downtown Eastside 674 a year in fiscal 1997–98 to 2000–01 against 370 in 2001–02 to 2002–03 (45.1%); heroin destined for Canada seized 184 kg a year against 67 kg (63.6%). No intervals or statistical tests.
key_findings.note: The percentages reproduce from the printed averages (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Figure 1 prints no values. Editors' reading at 300 dpi (approximate): drug-induced deaths in British Columbia about 399 (1998), 272 (1999), 218 (2000), 221 (2001), 169 (2002) and 186 (2003); naloxone-requiring responses in the Downtown Eastside about 732 (fiscal 1997–98), 840 (1998–99), 655 (1999–2000), 464 (2000–01), 388 (2001–02) and 350 (2002–03); heroin seized about 234, 142, 177, 94, 46 and 60 kg (1998 to 2003). Means by period from these readings: 296 and 192 deaths, 673 and 369 responses, 184 and 67 kg, each within 1 of Table 1.
key_findings.note: Bar tops read inside the 0.96-point bar outlines (the outer edge of a bar reads about 2 deaths, 4 responses or 1 kg higher) against the fitted axis ticks; cross-checked against the bar rectangles drawn in the PDF, which agree within 1. Approximate to about ±1 death, ±2 responses and ±0.5 kg.

key_findings.finding: Timing, from the Figure 1 readings (editors' calculations): deaths fell about 45% from 1998 to 2000, were about the same in 2001 as in 2000 and lower in 2002 and 2003; naloxone-requiring responses peaked in fiscal 1998–99 and fell every year after, fiscal 2000–01 already about 45% below the peak; seizures, after a fall from 1998 to 1999 and a rise in 2000, fell about 47% from 2000 to 2001 and again to 2002, with 2003 a little higher, so that every year from 2001 was below every earlier year. The paper does not comment on the falls before 2001.

Cohort: 1,587 participants gave 13,609 observations (May 1996 to December 2004); daily heroin injection was less likely in 2001–04 than in 1996–2000, adjusted odds ratio 0.55 (95% CI 0.50 to 0.61), P<0.001; in the same model current methadone use 0.43 (0.37 to 0.51), daily cocaine injection 2.32 (2.08 to 2.60), daily crack use 1.85 (1.65 to 2.06) and sex-trade involvement 1.34 (1.20 to 1.52); age, Downtown Eastside residence, Aboriginal ethnicity and gender also in the model, estimates not shown.

Shares of the cohort reporting daily use, by two-year period (the text's breakdown of 1997–2004 by quarter): 36.5% (1997/98), 32.6% (1999/00), 23.3% (2001/02) and 20.8% (2003/04); no counts, denominators or yearly values, so 2001 is not shown apart from 2002. Other drugs did not fall similarly, and methamphetamine use rose significantly (data not shown).

Coverage: the routine series end in 2003 (fiscal 2002–03 for naloxone) and the cohort in December 2004; no figure is given for 2005, for Vancouver's overdose deaths or for any area smaller than the Downtown Eastside, and supervised injection is not mentioned.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data sources (pp. 690–691); Results (p. 691); Figure 1 (p. 692); whole paper searched

key_findings.finding: Limitations as the authors state them: overdose statistics and seizure data may be poor proxies for heroin use, and the measures were not counted at the same level; fiscal years put 4 months of post-shortage data in the before period for naloxone; Canada has no standardized longitudinal measures of street heroin purity; other studies (cited) found ambulance and overdose mortality statistics to correlate strongly with street purity.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph (p. 693, right column, continued on p. 694)

key_findings.finding: Authors' conclusions: deaths and naloxone use fell markedly in western Canada at about the time of the Australian shortage, corroborated by the cohort's fall in heroin use; seizures fell by more than 60%; because Canada did not increase supply-reduction efforts, external global heroin supply forces deserve much greater investigation and credence as an explanation of the Australian shortage. They acknowledge that supply may instead have been diverted elsewhere or production switched to other drugs such as methamphetamine.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 692, continued on p. 693) and 6th paragraph (p. 694)

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives the after period for seizures as 2000–03 (Results, 3rd paragraph), while Table 1 and the abstract give 2001–03.
reporting_issues.consequence: A misprint in the text: the Figure 1 readings for 2001–03 average about 67 kg, as in Table 1; with 2000 included the mean would be about 94 kg (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: The Table 1 footnote dates the naloxone before period from fiscal '199–98' (the Methods and Results say 1997–98), and the table's column heads (1998–2000, 2001–03) do not describe the naloxone row, which compares four fiscal years with two.
reporting_issues.consequence: The naloxone comparison covers different years from the other two rows; it has to be read with the footnote.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract places the naloxone series in British Columbia; the Methods, Table 1 and Figure 1 give it for Vancouver's Downtown Eastside only.
reporting_issues.consequence: The naloxone figures describe one neighbourhood, not the province.

reporting_issues.issue: The routine series are called rates (the annual total event rate, the annual overdose mortality rate, the annual rate of naloxone use) but are yearly counts with no population denominator.
reporting_issues.consequence: Population change over 1998–2003 is not taken into account; the falls are falls in counts.

reporting_issues.issue: Two references do not match the statements they support: reduced heroin availability on Vancouver's streets, said to be widely reported in the media, cites a study of HIV viral rebound on antiretroviral drugs (ref. 17); the interest of drug policy-makers in the Australian supply-reduction efforts cites a study of self-perceived HIV risk and seroconversion (ref. 18).
reporting_issues.consequence: No source is given for media reports of reduced heroin availability in Vancouver; the statement rests on the authors' word.

reporting_issues.issue: The cohort's breakdown of 1997–2004 by quarter is four two-year periods, given as shares without counts or a stated denominator (people or interviews); the outcome is called daily heroin use in the Methods and Results text and daily heroin injection in the abstract and Table 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: The yearly course of daily heroin injection, including 2001 on its own, cannot be recovered from the paper.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), Addiction 101, pp. 689–695 (all 7 pages read in a text extraction and checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi; Tables 1 and 2 also at 300 dpi; Figure 1 rendered at 300 dpi and its 18 bars read by pixel measurement against the axis ticks, inside the bar outlines, and cross-checked against the bar rectangles drawn in the PDF; acknowledgements and all 29 references). No supplement. The figure's bars and axes are vector drawings; only its axis labels are an embedded image.
